atoms.note: Latin 'quinque' → 'cinco/cinq/cinque'; English 'five' and German 'fünf' show the Germanic 'f' for the same root *pénkʷe (think 'penta-' in Greek loanwords).
Romance 'qu-' forms (cuatro, quatre, quattro, quatro) all come from Latin 'quattuor'; English 'four' and German 'vier' kept the 'f/v' Germanic reflex of the same *kʷetwóres.

Romance 'number' (número, nombre, numero, número) and English 'number' all come from Latin 'numerus' — root of 'numeral', 'enumerate', 'numerous'. German 'Zahl' is Germanic (cf. 'tale', a count). A canon-tier word tying to the mathematics branch.

example.it: Il sette è il mio numero.

atoms.note: Romance '1' all descend from Latin 'unus'; English 'one' and German 'eins' are the Germanic branch of the same Indo-European root *óynos.

Spanish 'negro', French 'noir', Italian 'nero' all come from Latin 'niger' — root of 'denigrate'. Portuguese commonly uses 'preto' (from Latin 'apprehensus', pressed-tight/dense). English 'black' and German 'schwarz' are Germanic.

Two families here: Spanish/Portuguese 'azul' is from Arabic 'lāzaward' (lapis lazuli), while French 'bleu', Italian 'blu', English 'blue', German 'blau' all share the Germanic root *blēwaz. Latin had no single common word; 'caeruleus' (sky-blue) is the classical term.
Romance 'green' (verde, vert, verde, verde) all come from Latin 'viridis' — root of 'verdant', 'verdure'. English 'green' and German 'grün' share a Germanic root with 'grow' and 'grass'.

French 'enfant' and English 'infant' both come from Latin 'infans' (literally 'not speaking'). Portuguese 'criança' is from Latin 'creare' (to create — cf. 'creature'). Spanish 'niño' and Italian 'bambino' are nursery words. German 'Kind' (cf. 'kin', 'kindergarten') is Germanic.
Latin 'pater' (root of 'paternal', 'patriarch') gives padre/père/padre/pai. English 'father' and German 'Vater' come from the same *ph₂tḗr — the Latin 'p' became Germanic 'f' by Grimm's Law.
Romance 'friend' (amigo, ami, amico) is from Latin 'amicus', built on 'amare' (to love) — the same root as 'amiable' and 'amity'. English 'friend' and German 'Freund' are Germanic.

Romance 'man' (hombre, homme, uomo, homem) all come from Latin 'homo' (human being) — root of 'human', 'homage', 'Homo sapiens'. The silent Spanish/Portuguese 'h-' is the old Latin 'h'. English 'man' and German 'Mann' are Germanic.

Spanish 'pájaro' and Portuguese 'pássaro' come from Latin 'passer' (sparrow). Italian 'uccello' and French 'oiseau' come from Latin 'avicellus', a diminutive of 'avis' (root of 'aviary', 'aviation'). English 'bird' and German 'Vogel' are Germanic.

Almost every European 'cat' (gato, chat, gatto, gato, Katze, cat) descends from Late Latin 'cattus'. This word spread across the whole continent with the domestic cat itself — one of the most uniform cognates in the deck.
Romance 'bread' (pan, pain, pane, pão) all come from Latin 'panis' — the root of 'pantry', 'companion' (one you share bread with), and 'empanada'. English 'bread' and German 'Brot' are Germanic.

Romance 'big' (grande, grand, grande, grande) all come from Latin 'grandis' — root of 'grand', 'grandeur'. Latin's other word, 'magnus' (root of 'magnify', 'magnitude'), survives in scientific vocabulary. English 'big' / German 'groß' are Germanic.

example.fr: La route est longue, le chemin long.
example.it: La strada è lunga, il cammino lungo.
